3× [[Big Ten Conference football individual honors#Dave McClain Coach of the Year|Big Ten Coach of the Year]] (1994, 2005, 2008) | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 2007 | CFBHOF_id = 2207 }} '''Joseph Vincent Paterno''' ({{IPAc-en|p|ə|ˈ|t|ɜr|n|oʊ}}; December 21, 1926 – January 22, 2012), sometimes referred to as '''JoePa''', was an American [[college football]] player, [[athletic director]], and coach. He was the [[head coach]] of the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]] from 1966 to 2011. With 409 victories, Paterno is the most victorious coach in [[NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision|NCAA FBS]] history. He recorded his [[2011 Penn State Nittany Lions football team#October 29 vs. Illinois|409th victory on October 29, 2011]]; his career ended with his dismissal from the team on November 9, 2011, as a spend time around Sandusky until months before his arrest.'}} Paterno was born in [[Brooklyn, New York]]. He attended [[Brown University]], where he played football both ways as the [[quarterback]] and a [[cornerback]]. He had originally planned on going to law school, but he was instead hired in 1950 as an assistant football coach at Penn State. He was persuaded to do this by his college coach [[Rip Engle]], who had taken over as Penn State's head coach. In 1966, Paterno was named as Engle's successor. He soon coached the team to two undefeated regular seasons in [[1968 NCAA University Division football season|1968]] and [[1969 NCAA University Division football season|1969]]. The team won two national championships—in [[1982 NCAA Division I-A football season|1982]] and [[1986 NCAA Division I-A football season|1986]]. Paterno coached five undefeated teams that won major bowl games, and in 2007 he was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as a coach. During his career, he led the Nittany Lions to 37 bowl appearances with 24 wins while turning down offers to coach [[National Football League]] (NFL) teams that included the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and the [[New England Patriots]]. Paterno's coaching career ended abruptly in 2011, shortly before his death, when the [[Penn State Board of Trustees]] terminated his contract in response to a child sex abuse scandal involving Paterno's former defensive coordinator [[Jerry Sandusky]].{{cite news |title=Paterno and Spanier both out at Penn State |author=Michael Sanserino |url= http://www.post-gazette.com/stories/local/breaking/paterno-and-spanier-both-out-at-penn-state-323036/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140113082534/http://www.post-gazette.com/breaking/2011/11/09/Paterno-and-Spanier-both-out-at-Penn-State/stories/201111090216 |url-status= dead |archive-date= January 13, 2014 |newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |date=November 9, 2011 |access-date=November 19, 2011}} An investigation conducted by former [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] director [[Louis Freeh]] reported that Paterno concealed information relating to Sandusky's abuse of a young boy.Ken Belson, [https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/13/sports/ncaafootball/13pennstate.html "Abuse Scandal Inquiry Damns Paterno and Penn State"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', July 13, 2012.{{cite news | agency=Associated Press| title=Joe Paterno may have faced charges | url= https://www.espn.com/chicago/ncf/story/_/id/8164487/legal-experts-say-joe-paterno-faced-charges-freeh-report| date=July 13, 2012 | access-date=July 13, 2012}}{{cite web|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131213142810/http://www.statecollege.com/news/columns/holly-swanson-the-problem-with-paternoblame,1118249/ |url=http://www.statecollege.com/news/columns/holly-swanson-the-problem-with-paternoblame,1118249/ |url-status=dead|first=Holly |last=Swanson|title=The Problem with Paterno-Blame|archive-date=December 13, 2013|date=Aug 23, 2012|publisher=StateCollege.com|quote=The proof that Paterno and the others intentionally concealed Sandusky's actions is a stretch, at best. The most damning evidence is a string of out-of-context emails. Unfortunately, the people who wrote these emails were never interviewed during the Freeh investigation, leaving it up to the reader to decide what they meant.}} A critique of the Freeh report, commissioned by the Paterno family, disputed Paterno's involvement in the alleged cover-up.{{cite news |title=Critique of the Freeh Report: The Rush to Injustice Regarding Joe Paterno |author1=Wick Sollers |author2=Mark Jensen |author3=Alan Dial |author4=Drew Crawford |url=http://www.paterno.com/Resources/Docs/SOLLERS_FINAL_REPORT_2-9-2013.pdf |access-date=November 27, 2015 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304191723/http://www.paterno.com/Resources/Docs/SOLLERS_FINAL_REPORT_2-9-2013.pdf |url-status=dead }} In 2012, the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] vacated all of Penn State's wins from 1998 through 2011 as part of its punishment.{{cite news | url = https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/8191027/penn-state-hit-60-million-fine-4-year-bowl-ban-wins-dating-1998 | title = Penn State sanctions: $60M, bowl ban | work = [[ESPN]] |date = July 23, 2012 | access-date = July 23, 2012}} State Senator [[Jake Corman]] used the Freeh report as a basis to sue the NCAA, asserting that both Freeh and the NCAA had collaborated and failed to follow due process. Corman released emails showing "regular and substantive" contact between NCAA officials and Freeh's investigators, suggesting that Freeh's conclusions were orchestrated.{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/ncaaf-dr-saturday/emails-show-ncaa-worked-with-louis-freeh-in-penn-state-investigation-172215768.html|title=Emails show NCAA worked with Louis Freeh in Penn State investigation|date=November 12, 2014|work=Yahoo Sports|access-date=May 7, 2016}} In a 2015 legal settlement with Penn State, the NCAA reversed its decision and restored all 111 wins to Paterno's record.[https://www.si.com/college-football/2015/01/16/joe-paterno-penn-state-wins-restored Joe Paterno's Penn State wins restored]. "They had wildly different understandings about what was happening around them at that time.'}} ==Early life and education== Paterno was born December 21, 1926, in [[Brooklyn]], New York City, the son of Florence de LaSalle Cafiero, a homemaker, and Angelo Lafayette Paterno, a law clerk.{{cite web|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/article-1G2-3436500453/paterno-joseph-vincent-joe.html|title=Paterno, Joseph Vincent ("Joe")|access-date=May 7, 2016}} His family was of [[Italian American|Italian ancestry]]. He spoke with a marked Brooklyn accent throughout his life. In 1944, Paterno graduated from [[Brooklyn Preparatory School]]. Six weeks later, he was drafted into the [[United States Army]] during [[World War II]]. Paterno spent a year in the Army before being discharged in time to start the 1946 school year at [[Brown University]], where his tuition was paid by [[Everett M. "Busy" Arnold|Busy Arnold]].{{cite book | title = Paterno by the Book | author = Joe Paterno with Berndard Absell | publisher = Random House | location = New York | isbn = 0-394-56501-0 | year = 1989 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/paternobybook00pate }}{{cite web |url=http://wcfcourier.com/sports/college/iowa/article_677e81fa-a9b9-11de-a0ef-001cc4c03286.html |title=How Well Do You Know JoePa? |date=September 25, 2009 |access-date=October 3, 2010 |first=Don| last=Doxsie| work=[[Waterloo Daily Courier]]|location=Waterloo, Iowa| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111109234129/http://wcfcourier.com/sports/college/iowa/article_677e81fa-a9b9-11de-a0ef-001cc4c03286.html | archive-date=November 9, 2011|url-status=live}} At Brown University, Paterno was a member of [[Delta Kappa Epsilon]] fraternity.{{cite press release | title = DKE Mourns Loss of Brother Joe Paterno | publisher = Delta Kappa Epsilon International Fraternity | date = January 22, 2012 | url = http://dke.org/news.php?nid=1573 | access-date = January 22, 2012 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120808182713/http://dke.org/news.php?nid=1573 | archive-date = August 8, 2012 | df = mdy-all }} He played quarterback and cornerback for the [[Brown Bears football|Bears]], and he shares the career record for interceptions (14) with Greg Parker.{{cite web|url=http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/brow/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/FootballMediaGuide.pdf|title=2005 Brown University Football Media Guide|publisher=Brown University Sports Information Department|access-date=December 28, 2006|year=2005|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025083256/http://graphics.fansonly.com/photos/schools/brow/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/FootballMediaGuide.pdf|archive-date=October 25, 2012|url-status=dead}} Paterno graduated as an English literature major in 1950.{{cite news|last1=Dufresne|first1=Chris|title=Joe Paterno dies at 85; transformed Penn State into football power|url=https://www.latimes.com/local/obituaries/la-me-joe-paterno1-20120123-story.html|access-date=November 5, 2015|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=January 23, 2012}} ==Career== ===Penn State Nittany Lions=== {{expand section|date=December 2019}} {{Further|Penn State Nittany Lions}} Paterno had been accepted to [[Boston University School of Law]], and was planning to attend before changing his mind and deciding to coach at [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State]].{{cite news|last1=Wogenrich|first1=Mark|title=Former Penn State coach Paterno dead at 85|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2012/01/22/former-penn-state-coach-paterno-dead-at-85/|access-date=November 5, 2015|work=[[The Morning Call]]|date=January 22, 2012}} After hearing of his career choice, his father asked, "For God's sake, what did you go to college for?"{{cite news|last=Lopresti|first=Mike|title=Paterno's run at Penn State is one long journey|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/columnist/lopresti/2008-12-17-lopresti-paterno_N.htm|access-date=September 4, 2010|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|date=December 17, 2008}} Paterno joined [[Rip Engle]] as an assistant coach at Penn State in [[1950 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|1950]]; Engle had coached five seasons, from 1944 to 1949, at [[Brown University]]. In June [[1964 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|1964]], Paterno was promoted to associate coach, the top assistant coaching position.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=tyoNAAAAIBAJ&pg=7250%2C3177042 |newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |agency=Associated Press |title=Joe Paterno is promoted |date=June 18, 1964 |page=33 }} In 1966, when Engle announced his retirement,{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=5UANAAAAIBAJ&pg=6852%2C2719965|newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] | last=Jordan |first=Jimmy |title=Engle's exit completes Big 3 'sweep' |date=February 19, 1966|page=12 }} Penn State University announced Paterno as his successor the following day.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_KQtAAAAIBAJ&pg=5240%2C2360808|newspaper=[[Reading Eagle]] |agency=Associated Press |title=Joe Paterno named Penn State coach|date=February 20, 1966 |page=57}} [[File:Joseph Paterno, 1976.png|thumb|200x200px|Paterno, {{Circa|1976}}]] Over his coaching career, Paterno had one Heisman Trophy winner, [[John Cappelletti]], who earned the award in 1973. Penn State football struggled from 2000 to 2004, with an overall 26–33 record in those years and Paterno became the target of criticism from some Penn State faithful. Many in the media attributed Penn State's struggles to Paterno's advancing age. He had no apparent plans to retire, and contingents of fans and alumni began calling for him to step down. Paterno rebuffed all of this and stated he would fulfill his contract until it expired in 2008.{{cite news|title=Paterno driven to revive Lions|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=o5MNAAAAIBAJ&pg=2326,6489049|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|first=Ray|last=Fittipaldo|date=December 20, 2003|access-date=October 27, 2008|page=D-1}}{{Dead link|date=October 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Reflecting the growth in Penn State's stature, [[Beaver Stadium]] was expanded six times during his tenure, increasing in size from 46,284 in 1966 to 106,572 in 2001. During a speech in [[Pittsburgh]] on May 12, 2005, Paterno announced that he would consider retirement if the [[2005 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|2005 football team]] had a disappointing season. "If we don't win some games, I've got to get my rear end out of here", Paterno said in a speech at the Duquesne Club. "Simple as that".{{cite news |url=http://www.gainesville.com/article/20050514/GATORS20/50514005|title=Paterno puts career on line|date=May 13, 2005|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|last=Harlan|first=Chico|access-date=April 4, 2007}} Penn State finished the season with a record of 11–1 and were champions of the [[Big Ten]] in 2005. They defeated Florida State 26–23 in triple overtime in the [[2006 Orange Bowl]]. The 2009 season was Paterno's 44th as [[head coach]] of the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Nittany Lions]], passing [[Amos Alonzo Stagg]] for the most years as head coach at a single institution in Division I.[http://www.gopsusports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/paterno_joe00.html Joe Paterno] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180727175000/http://www.gopsusports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/paterno_joe00.html |date=July 27, 2018 }} GoPSUSports.com Paterno's abbreviated [[2011 NCAA Division I FBS football season|2011 season]] was his 62nd on the Penn State coaching staff, which gave him the record for most seasons for any football coach at a single university. From 2002 onward, Penn State faced a litany of players' off-the-field legal problems, which included 46 Penn State football players facing 163 criminal charges, of which 118 charges were dismissed or not proven, according to an [[ESPN]] analysis of Pennsylvania court records and reports.{{cite news | url=https://www.espn.com/espn/otl/news/story?id=3504915 | title=Has Penn State's on-field progress led to off-field problems? | first=Paula | last=Lavigne | publisher=ESPN | date=July 27, 2008 | access-date=November 6, 2011}}{{cite news | url=http://www.altoonamirror.com/page/content.detail/id/509555.html?nav=5017 | title=JoePa, PSU exposed by ESPN | first=Cory | last=Giger | newspaper=The Altoona Mirror | location=Altoona, PA | date=July 28, 2008 | access-date=November 6, 2011 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120819151507/http://www.altoonamirror.com/page/content.detail/id/509555.html?nav=5017 | archive-date=August 19, 2012 | df=mdy-all }} The [[Pennsylvania State Employees' Retirement System]] (SERS) revealed Paterno's salary in November 2007 as $512,664. He was paid $490,638 in 2006.{{cite news|title=Paterno's salary released to public|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=4215919|agency=Associated Press|date= May 29, 2009|access-date=January 1, 2011 | publisher = ESPN }} "I'm paid well, I'm not overpaid," Paterno said during an interview with reporters Wednesday before the salary disclosure. "I got all the money I need".{{cite news| url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/college/football/bigten/2007-11-29-paterno-salary_N.htm | work=[[USA Today]] | title=State: Joe Paterno's salary around $500,000 | date=November 30, 2007}} Paterno was known for his gameday image — thick glasses, rolled-up dress slacks (by his admission, to save on cleaning bills), white socks and Brooklyn-tinged speech.[[Ivan Maisel|Maisel, Ivan]]. [https://www.espn.com/college-football/story/_/id/7212678/penn-state-nittany-lions-coach-joe-paterno-legacy Joe Paterno's Penn State legacy]. [[ESPN]], November 9, 2011. ====Bowls and championships==== [[File:Joe Paterno runs out with team crop.jpg|thumb|Paterno jogs out with his team before the start of a game in September 2007]] Paterno holds an official NCAA total of 18 bowl victories. He holds the NCAA record for total bowl appearances with 37.{{cite news|title=Paterno says he has no plans to leave Penn State|publisher=ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=2685245|date=December 4, 2006|access-date=April 5, 2007}} He had a bowl record of 24 wins, 12 losses, and 1 tie following a defeat in the [[2011 Outback Bowl]]. Paterno was the first coach with the distinction of having won each of the four major bowls — Rose, Orange, Fiesta, and Sugar — as well as the Cotton Bowl Classic, at least once. Penn State won at least three bowl games in each of the four decades in which Paterno coached the entire decade, from 1970 thru 2009. Paterno led Penn State to two [[NCAA Division I-A national football championship|national championships]] (1982 and 1986) and five undefeated, untied seasons (1968, 1969, 1973, 1986, and 1994). Four of his unbeaten teams (1968, 1969, 1973, and 1994) won major bowl games and were not awarded a national championship. Under Paterno, Penn State won the [[Orange Bowl]] (1968, 1969, 1973 and 2005), the [[Cotton Bowl Classic]] (1972 and 1974), the [[Fiesta Bowl]] (1977, 1980, 1981, 1986, 1991, and 1996), the [[Liberty Bowl]] (1979), the [[Sugar Bowl]] (1982), the [[Aloha Bowl]] (1983), the [[Holiday Bowl]] (1989), the Citrus Bowl (1993 and 2010), the [[Rose Bowl Game]] (1994), the [[Outback Bowl]] (1995, 1998 and 2006), and the [[Alamo Bowl]] (1999 and 2007). After Penn State joined the [[Big Ten Conference]] in 1993, the Nittany Lions under Paterno won the [[Big Ten Conference football champions|Big Ten championship]] three times (1994, 2005 and 2008). Paterno saw [[Tony Johnson (wide receiver)|Tony Johnson]] catch a pass for a first down with both feet in bounds on the stadium's video replay board, but the play was ruled an incompletion.
